opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting divergences in the field right now, because both teams are very strong but have made quite different bets about where the bottleneck really is.

Physical Intelligence, at least from what they've shown publicly, has leaned heavily on data collected on actual robots: teleoperation across many embodiments, many tasks, and increasingly real homes and other messy environments. The logic is that data on the robot is the highest-fidelity signal you can get. The action space matches, the dynamics match, and you don't have to worry much about the gap between how a human moves and how a robot moves. The cost is that it's expensive and slow to scale. Every hour of data needs hardware, an operator, and maintenance.

Generalist has made a much more aggressive bet on scale. Their approach is closer to wearable or handheld collection devices, where people perform tasks in the real world and you capture the interaction directly. You can deploy far more collectors far more cheaply, so the volume can go up by orders of magnitude. And what they're really trying to show is that there's a scaling law in physical interaction data, similar to what we saw with language, where more data and bigger models keep improving in predictable ways.

My view is that the two routes will converge rather than one simply winning. Large-scale, cheap, human-centric data is very good for learning the broad prior: what objects are, how things move, what a sensible manipulation looks like. But it has gaps, especially in fine force control and the specific embodiment details. Robot-collected data is very good at closing that last-mile gap. So I expect a pyramid: a huge base of low-cost, diverse interaction data, possibly including video and simulation; a middle layer of embodiment-aligned data from devices like grippers that mimic the robot's hand; and a thinner, high-quality top layer of real robot data plus data from deployment and autonomous practice, maybe with RL on top.

The part I'd watch most closely is the data flywheel after deployment. Once robots are actually doing useful work, the data they generate themselves, including failures and corrections, may end up more valuable than anything collected by hand. Whoever closes that loop first will probably have the real advantage, more than whoever picked the better collection device at the start.

From my own perspective, coming from vision and generative models, I'd also add that world models and generated data will become a third leg. They won't replace real data, but they can multiply its value, by augmenting scenarios, evaluating policies, and letting the model "imagine" variations it never saw. So I don't see it as a binary choice between teleoperation and wearables. It's really a question of how you compose different data sources, and that recipe is still being figured out.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they actually represent two fairly different bets, and it's worth separating them.

Physical Intelligence's route is, in some sense, the more "orthodox" one. They're collecting a lot of teleoperation data on real robots — real hardware, real environments, a human in the loop demonstrating the task. The logic is very close to what worked in language: get as much high-quality, in-domain data as you can, scale the model, and let generalization emerge. The advantage is that the data is exactly what the robot needs at deployment time — same embodiment, same action space, same sensor noise. The cost is that it's expensive and slow. Every hour of data is an hour of a human operating a robot, and you can't parallelize that the way you can scrape the internet.

Generalist's route is more about going upstream of the robot. The idea is that human behavior itself — people doing things with their hands, in the real world, at enormous scale — is the real data source, and the robot-specific data is a much smaller layer on top. So you collect from humans first, with handheld devices or wearable setups that don't require a robot in the loop at all, and then you solve the embodiment gap afterwards. That gives you a data flywheel that's potentially orders of magnitude cheaper. The risk is obvious: humans are not robots. The hand is different, the kinematics are different, and the gap between "what a human did" and "what a robot can execute" is not trivial.

How do I see them evolving? I actually think they converge. Physical Intelligence will have to bring in cheaper sources — human video, simulation, cross-embodiment data — because pure teleoperation doesn't scale to the level you need for true generality. And Generalist will have to collect more real robot data, because at some point the embodiment gap can only be closed by actually touching the world with the robot. So the question is less "which route wins" and more "what's the right ratio," and what's the right architecture for mixing data with very different levels of fidelity.

If I had to make one prediction, it's that the winning recipe looks like a pyramid: a huge base of cheap human and internet-scale data for priors about objects, physics, and intention, a middle layer of simulation and cross-embodiment data, and a small, carefully curated tip of real robot data for alignment to the actual hardware. Both companies are building toward that pyramid, they just started from opposite ends.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a question of where you put the cost of collecting data. Do you collect directly on the robot, where the data is closely matched to what it needs to do, or do you collect more broadly and then solve the problem of transferring that experience to the robot?

I don’t have enough detail here to characterize Generalist’s and Physical Intelligence’s specific approaches confidently. But I would expect those two routes to converge. Broader collection can give you diversity—different environments, objects, and ways of completing a task. Robot data gives you the feedback that’s difficult to substitute for: whether a grasp actually holds, whether contact behaves as expected, and whether the robot can recover when something goes wrong.

The key question is how much useful capability you get from the next hour of data. As the models improve, I’d expect collection to become more targeted: identify where the policy fails, collect experience that addresses those failures, and then test whether it generalizes. The advantage will come from making that loop work reliably, rather than simply accumulating the largest dataset.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what kind of data will keep improving the model as you scale. You can collect a lot of robot hours, but if those hours repeat the same successful behavior, the value of each additional hour may fall quite quickly.

I would frame the two routes as different bets on how to get diversity efficiently. One emphasizes making data collection scalable; the other emphasizes connecting data closely to the robot’s actual capabilities. Those approaches can converge over time. A scalable collection system still needs to show that its data transfers to useful robot behavior, and a robot-centered approach still needs an economical way to expand coverage.

My expectation is that both will move toward a tighter feedback loop: train a model, identify where it fails, collect data specifically around those failures, and train again. Human demonstrations can provide a starting point, but eventually you want robot experience and human corrections to drive more of the improvement.

So I would watch how much less intervention the robot needs on unfamiliar tasks after each round of training. That tells you more about the data collection route than the total number of hours collected.
